impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations for claims against the government under 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is subject to American Pipe tolling, and whether California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc. implicitly overruled prior Federal Circuit precedent on this issue.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501's six-year statute of limitations is not subject to American Pipe tolling, affirming dismissal of claims by bank holding company FBOP and its subsidiaries arising from the 2008 financial crisis and government conservatorship of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. The court recognized that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's ANZ Securities decision.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity for the government as a defendant in financial crisis-related litigation, limiting the window for claimants to bring takings and breach of contract claims in the Court of Federal Claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Banks and financial institutions that relied on class action tolling to preserve individual claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims may find their claims time-barred, eliminating potential recovery for losses suffered during the 2008 financial crisis.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement when assessing copyright infringement damages, and whether the 'book of wisdom' doctrine permits reliance on post-infringement events to inflate damages beyond compensatory levels.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that courts need not defer to existing license agreement terms when calculating copyright infringement damages via hypothetical negotiation, but vacated the $12.68 million damages award in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government for its unauthorized copying of TETRA software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's affirmation that hypothetical negotiation is a permissible damages methodology not constrained by pre-existing license terms, potentially enabling higher damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling constrains how the 'book of wisdom' doctrine can be applied, limiting copyright holders from using post-infringement developments to inflate damages beyond actual compensatory levels.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations for a Defend Trade Secrets Act claim had expired before the plaintiff filed suit, where the plaintiff had knowledge of the alleged misappropriation more than three years before filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict and damages award in favor of Insulet for trade secret misappropriation under the DTSA, holding that EOFlow was entitled to judgment as a matter of law because the statute of limitations had expired before Insulet brought suit. Insulet had knowledge of former employees sharing proprietary CAD files and technical information with EOFlow more than three years before filing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from a strict application of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, providing a firm defense when plaintiffs delay in filing suit despite having knowledge of the alleged misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face significant risk of losing their claims if they do not promptly file suit upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation, even when the full scope of damages may not yet be apparent.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and rejecting damages models, and whether the jury verdict on breach of contract damages should be reinstated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, holding the district court improperly excluded Versata's damages expert and should reconsider two damages models. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury's award. The court affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation of automotive configuration software under both DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors benefit from the court's affirmation that trade secret misappropriation liability can attach when a licensee develops competing software during the license period, and that jury verdicts on breach of contract damages deserve deference.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk, and district courts' exclusion of damages expert testimony in trade secret cases will receive close appellate scrutiny.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar invalidity defenses that were not raised in a prior IPR petition, and whether the estoppel analysis must account for hindsight bias.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, holding that the court relied on insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The ruling narrows the scope of IPR estoppel by requiring courts to rigorously evaluate whether prior art reasonably could have been found by a skilled searcher without the benefit of hindsight.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a more rigorous standard for IPR estoppel, preserving the ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court litigation even after a prior IPR, particularly when newly discovered prior art is involved.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a more limited scope of protection from IPR estoppel, as defendants may more easily argue that prior art references were not reasonably discoverable at the time of the original IPR petition.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a jury verdict form that combines infringement findings for multiple patents into a single question requires vacatur, and whether the district court erred in its Alice step two analysis for patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million patent infringement judgment for building automation system patents because the verdict form improperly used a single question covering infringement for all asserted patents, making it impossible to determine which patents were infringed. The court also vacated and remanded for further proceedings on Alice step two eligibility for the '495 patent while affirming eligibility for other asserted patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must separately address infringement for each asserted patent, providing clearer grounds for challenging individual patent findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders risk losing jury verdicts if their proposed verdict forms aggregate infringement questions across multiple patents, requiring retrial even when the jury found infringement occurred.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent application's change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in a substituent definition constituted the correction of an obvious typographical error entitled to priority from the provisional application, or whether it added new matter breaking the priority chain.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's '953 patent as anticipated by Pfizer's public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (used in Paxlovid). The court held that changing 'C2' to 'C1' in a chemical substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error, breaking the priority chain to the provisional application and exposing the patent to Pfizer's intervening prior art disclosure.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers and competitors benefit from strict application of the written description requirement for priority claims, preventing patent holders from expanding claim scope through purported corrections to provisional applications.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies face significant risk that even minor discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional applications will break the priority chain, potentially exposing patents to intervening prior art and invalidation.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that retains the right to sue for infringement has constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit after granting an exclusive license to a third party.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement retains a sufficient exclusionary right to satisfy Article III standing. The court found that the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the rights granted to the exclusive licensee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license their patents exclusively can preserve standing to enforce their patents by carefully retaining the right to sue for infringement in their license agreements, providing flexibility in enforcement strategy.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face suits from patent owners even where an exclusive license exists, limiting their ability to challenge standing based on the ownership structure of the patents.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case qualified as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional under § 285, opening the door for potential attorney fee awards. The decision reinforces that data collection and processing claims in agricultural technology face significant eligibility challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in agricultural technology benefit from continued strict application of § 101, and the remand on exceptionality may enable fee recovery in cases involving patent-ineligible claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Agricultural technology companies face heightened risk that data collection and processing patents will be found patent-ineligible, and may face exceptional case findings leading to attorney fee awards against them.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent and whether the court could waive the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta for treating neurological disorders, upholding the district court's claim construction. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement, holding that the district court must require a bond pending appeal to protect the enjoined party from potential wrongful injunction damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmation of preliminary injunctions blocking generic entry, preserving market exclusivity during patent litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers are harmed by continued market exclusion, though the bond requirement provides some financial protection against wrongful injunctions. Branded companies must post security bonds, which may be substantial.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied motions for JMOL on non-infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain asserted patents related to non-uniform constellation designs in digital communications while affirming eligibility for others. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, including expert testimony on damages methodology. The case has significant implications for standards-essential patents in digital broadcasting technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers benefit from heightened scrutiny of patent eligibility for mathematical optimization patents, potentially reducing exposure to infringement claims for standard-compliant products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in communications technology face uncertainty as some patent claims survive eligibility challenges while others do not, requiring careful claim drafting to demonstrate technical improvement beyond abstract mathematical concepts.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade properly sustained Commerce's determination that debt-to-equity conversions by a foreign steel company conferred no countervailable benefit, and what deference is owed to Commerce's original versus protest determinations.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and reinstated Commerce's original determinations that debt-to-equity conversions by Korean steel producer Dongbu conferred countervailable benefits. The decision addresses the methodology for evaluating government equity infusions as countervailable subsidies under trade law, particularly when private investor prices are unavailable and equityworthiness must be assessed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers benefit from reinstatement of countervailing duty determinations, protecting against foreign government-subsidized competition. The decision reinforces Commerce's authority to find countervailable benefits in debt-to-equity conversions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign steel importers and their U.S. customers face renewed countervailing duties, increasing costs. Companies benefiting from government-backed debt restructuring may face greater scrutiny of such transactions as potential countervailable subsidies.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence where an entity that was not a party to the underlying patent litigation filed an IPR petition on the filing deadline of the actual defendant.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The case involved Qualcomm filing IPR petitions challenging patents asserted against Roambee on Roambee's filing deadline, despite Qualcomm not being a party to the underlying litigation. The court declined to review the denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer scrutiny of IPR petitions filed by third parties who may be acting as proxies for time-barred defendants, potentially preserving patent validity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to use third-party IPR filings as a defensive strategy face uncertainty, as the court left open but did not resolve questions about the propriety of such arrangements while vacating the underlying invalidity finding.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patent holder was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed non-infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents by Mylan's generic drug, holding that 'a pH of 13 or higher' is measured at the standard temperature recognized in the field (25°C). The court also upheld the finding that Actelion was barred from asserting the doctrine of equivalents. The decision has implications for ANDA litigation involving pH-dependent pharmaceutical formulations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers benefit from clear claim construction rules for scientific measurement terms, facilitating design-around strategies and ANDA filings for pH-sensitive pharmaceutical formulations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies face narrower patent protection when claims use scientific measurement terms without specifying conditions, as courts will apply field-standard measurement conditions that may exclude the accused products.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim terms reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform functions should be construed as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), particularly in light of the intervening Dyfan decision.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling for the '978 patent and remanded for further analysis of whether 'executable program code configured to' limitations invoke § 112(f) means-plus-function treatment under the court's intervening Dyfan precedent. The court affirmed the jury's invalidity finding for the '638 patent on anticipation grounds.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders may benefit from reconsideration of whether functional software claim terms invoke means-plus-function treatment, potentially avoiding indefiniteness invalidation under the evolving Dyfan framework.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies accused of infringement face continued uncertainty about the scope of software patent claims using functional language, as the standard for means-plus-function analysis continues to evolve.
